items.stem: In Git's model, what does each commit represent?

options.text: A snapshot of the tracked files at that point, with a link to its parent
options.rationale: Correct: Git stores snapshots of the project, each referencing its parent commit.

options.text: Only the text differences since the last commit
options.rationale: Git conceptually stores snapshots, not just diffs.

options.text: A copy of the remote server configuration
options.rationale: A commit records project content, not server configuration.

options.text: The list of branches in the repository
options.rationale: A commit is a project snapshot, not a branch list.

items.explanation: Correct: a Git commit is a snapshot of tracked content linked to its parent.

items.stem: Which TWO of Git's areas are involved when you run `git add` then `git commit`? (Select TWO)

options.rationale: Correct: git add moves changes into the staging area.
Correct: git commit records the staged snapshot into the repository.
Neither add nor commit contacts the remote; that needs push.
Garbage collection is not part of the add/commit flow.

items.explanation: Correct: add writes to the staging area and commit writes from there into the repository.

items.stem: Why is rewriting history with a force-push risky on a shared branch?

options.text: It can overwrite commits teammates have already based work on
options.rationale: Correct: force-pushing replaces shared history, which can discard or diverge from others' work.

options.text: It permanently deletes the remote repository
options.rationale: A force-push updates a branch; it does not delete the repository.

options.text: It converts the repository to read-only
options.rationale: Force-pushing does not change repository permissions.

options.text: It always resolves merge conflicts automatically

items.explanation: Correct: force-pushing shared history can clobber work others have already built on.
